Yeah... yeah, I do. I mean, I feel like I almost have to. The second I finally snap out of it and stop eating, this massive, suffocating wave of panic just hits me. It's like this ticking clock in my head. I can physically feel all that food just... sitting right there in my stomach, and I get so absolutely terrified that it's just sitting there turning into weight. But a lot of times, I'll go to the library. There's this really quiet floor near the top where the older books are, and the bathroom there is almost always completely empty. I just go in there and get rid of it. I hate sneaking around campus like that, constantly worrying if someone's going to walk in and hear me, but I just can't handle the thought of all those calories staying inside me. The anxiety is just so intense, I literally can't focus on my homework or anything else until I've gone to the bathroom and undone it...

I mean... I guess I'm probably at a normal weight? At least, that's what the scale says most of the time, but it's so hard to really trust it, you know? Like, I step on it and I see the number, and logically I know it falls into whatever the normal range is supposed to be for a guy my height, but when I look in the mirror, it just doesn't feel true. It feels like a lie. 

I constantly feel like I'm heavy, or like I'm just right on the edge of getting fat. Like, if I mess up even a little bit, if I don't get rid of the food fast enough, I'm just going to balloon up overnight. I spend so much time just staring at myself, pulling at my shirts to make sure they aren't clinging to my stomach, comparing myself to the other guys in my dorm who all seem to just effortlessly look fit and normal without even trying. It's exhausting. 

So, yeah, officially, I guess I'm normal weight, but I definitely don't feel normal. I don't feel like I fit in that category. I just feel like this bloated, heavy mess all the time, and I'm terrified that one day the scale is going to finally catch up to how I actually feel inside. It's like I'm just faking being a normal weight, and the throwing up is the only thing keeping the illusion going. I don't know... it's just really messed up how my brain sees it versus what the actual number is.

But then... if I catch my reflection in a dorm window, or just pass by a mirror in the student union, and I think my stomach looks even a little bit bigger, or my face looks rounder or puffier than the guys around me... it all just evaporates.

It literally feels like I failed at everything. The good grades don't matter. Being a good student doesn't matter. Being a good friend doesn't matter. All that matters in that split second is that I look wrong, and therefore I am wrong. It's this overwhelming sense of... of worthlessness, really. I just don't want anyone to see me. I want to hide in my room and not come out because I feel like everyone else is looking at me and thinking the exact same things I'm thinking about myself. They're thinking I'm heavy, or lazy, or whatever. 

It's like my entire value as a human being is completely dependent on whether my stomach is flat that day. And if it's not, then I'm nothing. I'm just a failure. And I hate that I think that way, I really do, because logically I know there's more to me than my body. I know I have a brain, I know I'm trying hard in school. But none of that logic stands a chance when I feel fat. The feeling just completely takes over and tells me that if I don't look perfect, I don't deserve to feel good about anything else in my life. So yeah... my weight is basically the only thing that dictates how I feel about myself on any given day.

Yeah, exactly. That's actually a huge part of why I finally decided to come in and talk to someone. Because it's not just like, "Oh, I was really hungry and I ate a big meal." It's so much scarier than that. It’s like... once I take that first bite, if I'm in my dorm late at night and my roommate is out, and I open a bag of chips or something, it's like I just disappear.

It's like I'm a passenger in my own body watching someone else do it. 

I'll go through the chips, then I'll find a box of cereal, then maybe some stale cookies I have shoved in my desk drawer, or I'll even go down to the vending machine in the lobby and buy four or five candy bars. I mean... I don't know if guilt is really the right word for that specific moment. I just keep repeating the same exact pattern, over and over, multiple days a week, and it's so exhausting trying to keep track of it all and hide it from my roommate for that many days in a row. Like, you'd think I'd get a break for just seven days, just one normal week where I don't end up hunched over in that library bathroom trying to be quiet, but no. It just never stops.\n\nDoctor: Do you exercise to try to burn off calories after one of these episodes?\n\nPatient: No, I don't really do that. I mean, I know some people probably do, like go for a run or hit the gym or whatever, but I just... I don't. Honestly, by the time the whole thing is over—like, after I've eaten all that food and then rushed to the bathroom to get rid of it—I am just completely wiped out. It's like my whole body just feels heavy and drained, you know? \n\nAnd on top of that, I'm just so focused on my classes right now. Or, well, I'm trying to be focused on my classes. Between the studying and the reading and just trying to keep my head above water with my coursework, and then dealing with this whole... cycle... taking up so much of my mental energy and time, I just can't imagine trying to fit in a workout on top of it all. I don't even really like exercising anyway, to be completely honest. I've never been the athletic type, not in high school, not now. So, no, I don't go to the campus gym or run around the quad or anything like that. The throwing up is really the only thing I do to try and fix it, because the panic is just so immediate, I need it gone right then and there. I couldn't handle waiting to burn it off even if I wanted to, which I don't. So yeah, just the throwing up. No exercise.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you are currently underweight, overweight, or at a normal weight?\n\nPatient: I mean... I guess I'm probably at a normal weight? At least, that's what the scale says most of the time, but it's so hard to really trust it, you know? Like, I step on it and I see the number, and logically I know it falls into whatever the normal range is supposed to be for a guy my height, but when I look in the mirror, it just doesn't feel true. It feels like a lie. \n\nI constantly feel like I'm heavy, or like I'm just right on the edge of getting fat. Like, if I mess up even a little bit, if I don't get rid of the food fast enough, I'm just going to balloon up overnight. I spend so much time just staring at myself, pulling at my shirts to make sure they aren't clinging to my stomach, comparing myself to the other guys in my dorm who all seem to just effortlessly look fit and normal without even trying. It's exhausting. \n\nSo, yeah, officially, I guess I'm normal weight, but I definitely don't feel normal. I don't feel like I fit in that category. I just feel like this bloated, heavy mess all the time, and I'm terrified that one day the scale is going to finally catch up to how I actually feel inside. It's like I'm just faking being a normal weight, and the throwing up is the only thing keeping the illusion going. I don't know... it's just really messed up how my brain sees it versus what the actual number is.\n\nDoctor: Is the fear of gaining weight something that is always on your mind, even when you're not in the middle of one of these eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Yeah, it really is. It’s... it’s honestly like a hum in the background of everything I do, all day long. Like, I can be having a completely normal day, you know? I’ll go to my morning classes, take my notes, maybe even feel pretty good about a quiz I just took or something. I’ll be having a decent day. But then... I don't know, I’ll be walking across campus, and I’ll just catch my reflection in the glass of one of the dorm windows, or even just in the mirror in the bathroom between classes. And if I look at myself and think my stomach looks even slightly bigger, or my face looks rounder than the other guys around me... it just ruins everything. \n\nIt’s like this instant, crushing weight. Suddenly, the fact that I did well on a quiz doesn't matter at all. It feels like I’ve just failed at everything, like my whole worth is tied up in how I look in that one second. And when that happens, I just... I don’t want anyone to see me. I want to pull my hoodie down, cross my arms over my stomach, and just disappear. I’ll start analyzing every single thing I ate that day, or what I ate the day before, and I’ll start comparing myself to literally every guy I walk past on the sidewalk. Like, 'Oh, his jawline is sharper than mine,' or 'His shirt fits him perfectly and mine is clinging to my sides.' \n\nIt’s so exhausting because I can’t just turn it off. Even when I’m sitting in a lecture hall, trying to focus on what the professor is saying, half my brain is thinking about how I’m sitting and if my posture is making my stomach roll, or if the person sitting next to me is judging how much space I’m taking up. It’s not just when I’m eating or throwing up. It’s literally all the time. It dictates what clothes I choose in the morning, where I sit in the dining hall, whether I even want to hang out with my friends on the weekend. If I feel 'fat' that day, I just won't go out. I’ll make up an excuse about having too much homework because the thought of people looking at me and thinking I’ve gained weight is just... I can't handle it. So, yeah, it's definitely always there. Always.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your worth as a person is tied to your weight or appearance?\n\nPatient: I mean... yeah. Yeah, I really do. I know it sounds messed up when I say it out loud, but it's like... it's exactly what I was just saying about the window reflection, you know? Like, I could literally be having the best day. I could ace a midterm, I could get a compliment from a professor, I could be feeling like I actually belong in college and I'm doing a good job. I can have a decent day in classes, and I'll feel smart, I'll feel capable. But then... if I catch my reflection in a dorm window, or just pass by a mirror in the student union, and I think my stomach looks even a little bit bigger, or my face looks rounder or puffier than the guys around me... it all just evaporates.\n\nIt literally feels like I failed at everything. The good grades don't matter. Being a good student doesn't matter. Being a good friend doesn't matter. All that matters in that split second is that I look wrong, and therefore I am wrong. It's this overwhelming sense of... of worthlessness, really. I just don't want anyone to see me. I want to hide in my room and not come out because I feel like everyone else is looking at me and thinking the exact same things I'm thinking about myself. They're thinking I'm heavy, or lazy, or whatever. \n\nIt's like my entire value as a human being is completely dependent on whether my stomach is flat that day. And if it's not, then I'm nothing. I'm just a failure. And I hate that I think that way, I really do, because logically I know there's more to me than my body. I know I have a brain, I know I'm trying hard in school. But none of that logic stands a chance when I feel fat. The feeling just completely takes over and tells me that if I don't look perfect, I don't deserve to feel good about anything else in my life. So yeah... my weight is basically the only thing that dictates how I feel about myself on any given day.\n\nDoctor: Is your fear of gaining weight the main reason you make yourself vomit after eating?\n\nPatient: Yeah... yeah, it absolutely is. It’s the only reason, really. Because when I have one of those moments where I just eat and eat... the panic that sets in right after is just, it's indescribable. It's like this overwhelming, suffocating terror. I can physically feel the food inside me, feeling so heavy and wrong, and my brain just starts screaming at me. Like, I can literally picture the food just sitting there in my stomach, turning into weight, turning into fat, right that very second. \n\nAnd I can't handle that thought. I just can't sit with it. So, after I eat like that, I usually end up rushing to find a bathroom so I can make myself throw up. If I'm back at my building, I'll use the dorm bathroom, but I always have to pace around and check if the guys on my hall are hanging out nearby, which is a whole other stressful thing because the walls are so thin. Or, a lot of times, I'll go up to a quiet floor of the library. You know, like the upper floors where the old reference books are and no one really goes unless it's finals week? There's a bathroom tucked away in the corner up there that's almost always empty. \n\nI'll just lock myself in a stall and make myself throw up, just to get it out. Because I am just so terrified that if I don't, the food is just sitting there turning into weight. It’s like a race against the clock in my head. If I don't get rid of it fast enough, it's going to be permanent, and I'll wake up the next day completely bloated and huge, and everyone will be able to tell. So the fear of that happening... yeah, that's exactly why I do it. I just have to stop the food from staying inside me.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you have no control over what you're eating or how much you're eating during these episodes?\n\nPatient: Yeah, exactly. That's actually a huge part of why I finally decided to come in and talk to someone. Because it's not just like, \"Oh, I was really hungry and I ate a big meal.\" It's so much scarier than that. It’s like... once I take that first bite, if I'm in my dorm late at night and my roommate is out, and I open a bag of chips or something, it's like I just disappear. \n\nThe rational part of my brain, the part that cares about my weight and my classes and everything we were just talking about, it just gets pushed aside. It feels like something else completely takes over my body. I'll be sitting there on my bed, cramming food into my mouth, and in my head, I'm literally screaming at myself. I'm thinking, \"What are you doing? Stop! You're going to regret this so much, you're going to have to go throw this up, just put the bag down!\" But my hands just keep moving. It's like I'm a passenger in my own body watching someone else do it. \n\nI'll go through the chips, then I'll find a box of cereal, then maybe some stale cookies I have shoved in my desk drawer, or I'll even go down to the vending machine in the lobby and buy four or five candy bars. I don't even taste it half the time. I'm not eating because it tastes good. I just keep chewing and swallowing and opening new wrappers, and I keep going and going until I physically cannot fit another bite into my stomach. I literally don't stop until it hurts so bad I can't even stand up straight, until I just can't stand it anymore. \n\nAnd the whole time, I'm so aware of how messed up it is, but I have absolutely zero power to stop it. It’s like a trance. I can't control what I'm grabbing, I can't control how fast I'm eating... it's just this frantic, desperate feeling. That total loss of control is just... it's terrifying. It makes me feel completely crazy, honestly, because I know I don't want to be doing it, but I just can't make myself stop.\n\nDoctor: Do you usually feel guilty or ashamed after one of these eating episodes, before you make yourself vomit?\n\nPatient: I mean... I don't know if guilt is really the right word for that specific moment. Like, I'm not sure I've ever really stopped to notice if I feel ashamed right then, because... well, the second I stop eating, when I literally can't take another bite, there isn't really room in my head for guilt. It's just pure, absolute panic. \n\nLike I was saying before, it's a race against the clock. So I'm not sitting on my bed thinking, \"Oh, I'm such a bad person, I'm so ashamed of myself.\" I don't have time for that. My brain just immediately shifts into this emergency override mode. I'll be looking at the empty wrappers—the chip bags, the candy wrappers, the cereal box, whatever is just scattered all over my bed—and I don't really feel guilty looking at them. I just feel completely terrified of what they represent, you know? It's like, I have to get this out of me *now*. \n\nI'll be grabbing my dorm keys, shoving the wrappers under my pillow so my roommate doesn't see them if he walks in, and then I'm cracking my door open to check the hallway. I'm listening to see if the guys next door are playing video games with their door open, or if anyone is walking up the stairs. And my heart is just pounding so hard I can actually hear it in my ears, and I'm usually sweating and kind of shaking. \n\nSo if you're asking if I sit there and feel ashamed before I go to the bathroom... I really don't think so. I haven't noticed feeling that way. It's just this frantic, tunnel-vision need to fix what I just did. Maybe the shame comes later, like way later when I'm finally back in my room and I'm trying to fall asleep and my throat hurts and I'm just so exhausted... but right in that gap between the eating and getting to the bathroom? No, I don't think I feel guilty then. I'm just way too scared.\n\n[Instruction]\n- Give candidates as ICD-10 codes, not disease names.\n- If the list changed from the previous candidates, say in \"note\" what this turn added or ruled out. I mean... days or weeks? No. Definitely not. I wish I could, honestly, but no, I've never made it anywhere near that long. 

Like I was just saying a minute ago, I try to restrict. I really, really try. I'll make all these elaborate plans in my head. I'll even write it down in my planner sometimes, right next to my assignment due dates, like, "Monday: water only. Tuesday: one apple and black coffee." I build it up in my head like I'm finally going to take control, like I'm going to go on this long fast and completely reset my body and finally be disciplined. 

But it never, ever lasts for days. I think the absolute longest I've ever made it was maybe... I don't know, maybe 36 hours? And that was only because I had a massive history paper due and I basically locked myself in the library and drank about six energy drinks and just rode the caffeine anxiety until I crashed. But usually? I can barely make it 24 hours. 

It's just... the pressure builds up way too fast. I'll get to the evening of day one, and I'll be sitting in my dorm, trying to read for my intro to psych class or whatever, and the hunger just turns into this deafening static in my head. I can't focus on the words on the page. I can't watch a video. I can't even hold a normal conversation with my roommate because all I'm thinking about is the fact that I'm not eating, and then suddenly, all I can think about is everything I *want* to eat. 

It's like a pressure cooker, you know? I try to lock the lid down tight and tell myself I'm going to starve for a week, but the steam just builds and builds until I completely snap. By Monday night, I'm just pacing the room, listening to my roommate breathe while he sleeps, just waiting for the coast to be clear so I can sneak down to the vending machines in the basement or walk over to the 24-hour convenience store. 

So, no, I don't have these long stretches where I'm just severely restricting. I wish I had that kind of willpower, as messed up as that sounds. For me, the restricting is really just... it's just the waiting period between the binges. It's just the setup for the next failure. It never lasts more than a day or so before the whole awful cycle just explodes all over again.

Not one. I just keep repeating the same exact pattern, over and over, multiple days a week, and it's so exhausting trying to keep track of it all and hide it from my roommate for that many days in a row. Like, you'd think I'd get a break for just seven days, just one normal week where I don't end up hunched over in that library bathroom trying to be quiet, but no. So, no, I don't go to the campus gym or run around the quad or anything like that. No exercise.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you are currently underweight, overweight, or at a normal weight?\n\nPatient: I mean... I guess I'm probably at a normal weight? At least, that's what the scale says most of the time, but it's so hard to really trust it, you know? I mean, I know I just talked about the weight thing, and that's huge, obviously. That's the main thing I'm focused on when I'm in that panic mode. But the control part... I don't know. Maybe? Like, my body did this thing I didn't want it to do, it ate all this food, and now I'm forcing it to undo it. \n\nBut honestly, in that moment, when I'm rushing to the bathroom and trying not to be seen by the guys in my hall, I'm not really analyzing my motivations like that. It's like... the loss of control leads to the food, the food leads to the fear of weight, and the fear of weight leads to the bathroom. It's just this one continuous loop. I'm sorry, I know that's probably not a very helpful answer. I just... I haven't really dissected it like that before. It's all just this one big, desperate reaction, you know?\n\nDoctor: When you make yourself vomit after one of these episodes, is it specifically to undo the calories you've just consumed?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, I mean... exactly. No, never. And honestly, that’s the part that just... it drives me completely crazy. Like, I’ve never been significantly low weight, not ever. I’ve always just been... average. Or at least, I feel like I'm massive, but I guess on paper I'm just normal. When I was in middle school and early high school, I was maybe a little chubby, which I absolutely hated, and I thought when I came to college and started... well, doing all this, that I would finally get really thin. But it just hasn't happened. 

I actually have this digital scale that I bought at Target the second week of freshman year, and I keep it shoved way back under my bed in its original box so my roommate doesn't see it. I pull it out, like, every single morning when he goes to his 8 AM calc class. I strip down to nothing, make sure I've gone to the bathroom first, and I stand on it, just praying the number will be drastically lower. Always.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your worth as a person is tied to your weight or appearance?\n\nPatient: I mean... yeah. Yeah, I really do. I know it sounds messed up when I say it out loud, but it's like... it's exactly what I was just saying about the window reflection, you know? Like, I could literally be having the best day. I could ace a midterm, I could get a compliment from a professor, I could be feeling like I actually belong in college and I'm doing a good job. I can have a decent day in classes, and I'll feel smart, I'll feel capable. But then... if I catch my reflection in a dorm window, or just pass by a mirror in the student union, and I think my stomach looks even a little bit bigger, or my face looks rounder or puffier than the guys around me... it all just evaporates.\n\nIt literally feels like I failed at everything. The good grades don't matter. Being a good student doesn't matter. Being a good friend doesn't matter. All that matters in that split second is that I look wrong, and therefore I am wrong. It's this overwhelming sense of... of worthlessness, really. I just don't want anyone to see me. I want to hide in my room and not come out because I feel like everyone else is looking at me and thinking the exact same things I'm thinking about myself. They're thinking I'm heavy, or lazy, or whatever. \n\nIt's like my entire value as a human being is completely dependent on whether my stomach is flat that day. And if it's not, then I'm nothing. I'm just a failure. And I hate that I think that way, I really do, because logically I know there's more to me than my body. I know I have a brain, I know I'm trying hard in school. But none of that logic stands a chance when I feel fat. The feeling just completely takes over and tells me that if I don't look perfect, I don't deserve to feel good about anything else in my life. So yeah... my weight is basically the only thing that dictates how I feel about myself on any given day.\n\nDoctor: Is your fear of gaining weight the main reason you make yourself vomit after eating?\n\nPatient: Yeah... yeah, it absolutely is. It’s the only reason, really. Because when I have one of those moments where I just eat and eat... the panic that sets in right after is just, it's indescribable. It's like this overwhelming, suffocating terror. I can physically feel the food inside me, feeling so heavy and wrong, and my brain just starts screaming at me. Like, I can literally picture the food just sitting there in my stomach, turning into weight, turning into fat, right that very second. \n\nAnd I can't handle that thought. I just can't sit with it. So, after I eat like that, I usually end up rushing to find a bathroom so I can make myself throw up. If I'm back at my building, I'll use the dorm bathroom, but I always have to pace around and check if the guys on my hall are hanging out nearby, which is a whole other stressful thing because the walls are so thin. Or, a lot of times, I'll go up to a quiet floor of the library. You know, like the upper floors where the old reference books are and no one really goes unless it's finals week? There's a bathroom tucked away in the corner up there that's almost always empty. \n\nI'll just lock myself in a stall and make myself throw up, just to get it out. Because I am just so terrified that if I don't, the food is just sitting there turning into weight. It’s like a race against the clock in my head. If I don't get rid of it fast enough, it's going to be permanent, and I'll wake up the next day completely bloated and huge, and everyone will be able to tell. So the fear of that happening... yeah, that's exactly why I do it. I just have to stop the food from staying inside me.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you have no control over what you're eating or how much you're eating during these episodes?\n\nPatient: Yeah, exactly. That's actually a huge part of why I finally decided to come in and talk to someone. Because it's not just like, \"Oh, I was really hungry and I ate a big meal.\" It's so much scarier than that. It’s like... once I take that first bite, if I'm in my dorm late at night and my roommate is out, and I open a bag of chips or something, it's like I just disappear. \n\nThe rational part of my brain, the part that cares about my weight and my classes and everything we were just talking about, it just gets pushed aside. It feels like something else completely takes over my body. I'll be sitting there on my bed, cramming food into my mouth, and in my head, I'm literally screaming at myself. I'm thinking, \"What are you doing? Stop! You're going to regret this so much, you're going to have to go throw this up, just put the bag down!\" But my hands just keep moving. It's like I'm a passenger in my own body watching someone else do it. \n\nI'll go through the chips, then I'll find a box of cereal, then maybe some stale cookies I have shoved in my desk drawer, or I'll even go down to the vending machine in the lobby and buy four or five candy bars. I don't even taste it half the time. I'm not eating because it tastes good. I just keep chewing and swallowing and opening new wrappers, and I keep going and going until I physically cannot fit another bite into my stomach. I literally don't stop until it hurts so bad I can't even stand up straight, until I just can't stand it anymore. \n\nAnd the whole time, I'm so aware of how messed up it is, but I have absolutely zero power to stop it. It’s like a trance. I can't control what I'm grabbing, I can't control how fast I'm eating... it's just this frantic, desperate feeling. That total loss of control is just... it's terrifying. It makes me feel completely crazy, honestly, because I know I don't want to be doing it, but I just can't make myself stop.\n\nDoctor: Do you usually feel guilty or ashamed after one of these eating episodes, before you make yourself vomit?\n\nPatient: I mean... I don't know if guilt is really the right word for that specific moment. Like, I'm not sure I've ever really stopped to notice if I feel ashamed right then, because... well, the second I stop eating, when I literally can't take another bite, there isn't really room in my head for guilt. It's just pure, absolute panic. \n\nLike I was saying before, it's a race against the clock. So I'm not sitting on my bed thinking, \"Oh, I'm such a bad person, I'm so ashamed of myself.\" I don't have time for that. My brain just immediately shifts into this emergency override mode. I'll be looking at the empty wrappers—the chip bags, the candy wrappers, the cereal box, whatever is just scattered all over my bed—and I don't really feel guilty looking at them. I just feel completely terrified of what they represent, you know? It's like, I have to get this out of me *now*. \n\nI'll be grabbing my dorm keys, shoving the wrappers under my pillow so my roommate doesn't see them if he walks in, and then I'm cracking my door open to check the hallway. I'm listening to see if the guys next door are playing video games with their door open, or if anyone is walking up the stairs. And my heart is just pounding so hard I can actually hear it in my ears, and I'm usually sweating and kind of shaking. \n\nSo if you're asking if I sit there and feel ashamed before I go to the bathroom... I really don't think so. I haven't noticed feeling that way. It's just this frantic, tunnel-vision need to fix what I just did. Maybe the shame comes later, like way later when I'm finally back in my room and I'm trying to fall asleep and my throat hurts and I'm just so exhausted... but right in that gap between the eating and getting to the bathroom? No, I don't think I feel guilty then. I'm just way too scared.\n\nDoctor: Do you make yourself vomit after these eating episodes specifically because you're afraid of gaining weight from the food you've eaten?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah... I mean, I think I just said that, but yes, absolutely. It's... it's the entire reason. Like I was saying, after one of those times where I just lose control and eat everything in sight, I usually end up in a bathroom somewhere, either in the dorm if I can sneak past the guys on my hall, or up on one of those quiet floors in the library where no one goes. And I make myself throw up because... well, because I am just so completely terrified that the food is just sitting there inside me, literally turning into weight right then and there. \n\nIt's like I can feel it happening, you know? Like this heavy, horrible feeling in my stomach, and my brain is just screaming that if I don't get it out right that second, it's going to stick to me and I'll be huge. So, yeah, I make myself sick because I'm just so incredibly scared of gaining weight from all that food. It's the only way I can make that panic stop, the only way I can feel like I've undone the damage, even though I know it's messed up. I just can't handle the thought of that food staying inside me.\n\nDoctor: Is the fear of gaining weight the only reason you purge after eating, or is it also because you feel like you've lost control over how much you've eaten?\n\nPatient: I mean...
